news_drafts.headline: Wandsworth forecasts £23.112m High Needs overspend, taking schools-funding deficit to £19.368m by March 2027
news_drafts.lead:
Wandsworth Council expects spending on support for children with special educational needs to run £23.112m over its budget this year, according to a report to its Schools Forum on 12 October. High needs (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities) is forecast to cost £93.363m against a budget of £70.250m. That is £10.610m more than last year's actual spending (outturn) of £82.753m.

After the in-year overspend of £16.112m on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools), the cumulative deficit is forecast to reach £19.368m by 31 March 2027. That figure starts from £3.255m carried forward, which assumes 90% of the earlier deficit is written off through the High Needs Stability Grant. The paper says the write-off does not address the gap between high needs funding and spending. A £6m underspend on early years and £1m on the schools block offset part of the overspend, but the paper says they "do not resolve the underlying High Needs funding gap".

Independent specialist placements are the largest driver, rising by £2.979m to £21.047m. The council funds about 404 full-time-equivalent places, against 254 in 2020-21, and the average cost has risen from about £34.3k to £52.0k. Education, health and care plans (EHCPs) have grown from 2,703 in 2021 to 3,584 in August 2026. High needs spending has more than doubled from £44.480m in 2019-20. The paper says the priority is to contain future growth through local sufficiency, inclusion, early intervention and placement management.
news_drafts.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026

news_drafts.headline: Wandsworth forecasts £0.688m treasury underspend as cash balances cover borrowing it had budgeted for
news_drafts.lead:
Wandsworth Council expects to spend £0.688m less than budgeted on treasury management (how it borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both) this year, according to the first quarterly budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) put to its Cabinet on 12 October 2026.

The saving comes from two sources. The budget assumed the council would need to borrow from outside, which the report called "the most prudent assumption". In practice the council can pay for its spending from its own cash, which removes the interest it would have paid on external loans. The cash it holds is also earning more than planned. The report says: "Interest earned on cash balances is therefore expected to be higher than budgeted for." It adds that there is "a possible rate increase in year".

The treasury saving is the main driver of a forecast net underspend of £0.276m in the finance budget, which has a notional budget of -£3.335m. The report describes it as a material offset to overspends in individual services.

news_drafts.headline: Wandsworth projects £4m overspend in children's social care, despite an Outstanding Ofsted rating
news_drafts.lead:
Wandsworth Council is projecting a £4m overspend in children's social care this financial year, its Finance Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told at its meeting on 8 October. The paper says "an overspend of £4m is currently being projected in this financial year" (2025/26).

The forecast comes after Ofsted, the schools and children's services inspectorate, rated the council's Children's Services Outstanding in May 2026. The papers give two main causes. One is the rising complexity of need among children looked after by the council and children with disabilities. The other is the cost of transport, which has grown as demand has risen for support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

The council says it is responding through early help and prevention, increasing local provision and improving how it commissions, or buys, places for children in care. The paper states that these measures "will take time to deliver", so they are not expected to remove the overspend within the current year.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Forecast includes £6m Early Years underspend and £1m Schools Block underspend, but paper states these 'do not resolve the underlying High Needs funding gap'
findings.detail: The £7m combined underspend provides partial offset to the £23.112m High Needs overspend. Early Years underspend is activity-led and subject to ongoing census review. The paper explicitly notes these offsets are insufficient and the priority must be to 'contain future growth through local sufficiency, inclusion, early intervention and robust placement management.'
findings.matters: Shows a broad DSG portfolio where some blocks underspend (often related to take-up volatility) while High Needs overruns massively; offsetting approach cannot be relied upon, requiring structural solutions.
findings.figures: £6m Early Years underspend; £1m Schools Block underspend; offset against £23.112m High Needs overspend
findings.quote: The £6m Early Years underspend and £1m Schools Block underspend provide a significant offset in FY 2026-27, but they do not resolve the underlying High Needs funding gap.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Post-16 EHCP demand forecast to accelerate, with growth concentrating in the 16-25 age range while school-age demand levels off
findings.detail: While some school-age EHCP cohorts are expected to level off, the 16-25 age range shows continued growth trajectory. Post-16 placements (Further Education and specialist) are typically funded for longer durations and carry higher average costs than school-age placements.
findings.matters: Signals that High Needs cost pressures will persist and likely increase beyond FY 2026-27; the shift to post-16 means longer-duration, higher-cost commitments that compound budget pressure.
findings.figures: Forecast shows continued growth in 16-25 cohort; Further Education forecast to increase by £1.079m; resource bases £0.870m
findings.quote: Forecasts indicate that future EHCP growth is increasingly concentrated within the 16 to 25 age range. Whilst demand across a number of school-age cohorts begins to level off over the medium term, the number of young people requiring post-16 support continues to increase. This will place additional pressure on Further Education provision and specialist post-16 placements, which are typically funded for longer durations and often carry higher average costs than mainstream school placements.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Mainstream top-up funding forecast to increase by £1.916m, with FTE growing 55% (1,130 vs 729 in 2020-21) despite overall school rolls declining
findings.detail: More pupils are requiring top-up funding in mainstream schools despite falling mainstream rolls, indicating both volume growth and increasing average cost per pupil (£12.7k vs £9.3k). This demonstrates that a larger proportion of the remaining mainstream pupil population requires additional support.
findings.matters: Shows the structural shift is not confined to specialist placements; mainstream settings are also absorbing cost pressures from higher-need cohorts, requiring investment in mainstream capacity and training.
findings.figures: £1.916m increase; 1,130 FTE vs 729 FTE (55% increase); average cost £12.7k vs £9.3k
findings.quote: Mainstream FTE has grown from approximately 729 in FY 2020-21 to 1,130 in FY 2026-27, while the average cost has increased from approximately £9.3k to £12.7k. This demonstrates that, despite falling school rolls, a larger number and proportion of pupils are requiring additional support in mainstream settings.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Independent specialist placements (£21.047m) are the largest High Needs cost driver, with FTE up 59% (404 vs 254 in 2020-21) and average cost up 51% (£52.0k vs £34.3k)
findings.detail: The £2.979m year-on-year increase reflects both volume growth and significant cost inflation. This is the single largest component of the £23.112m High Needs overspend. The average cost rise from £34.3k to £52.0k suggests both provider cost increases and potential mix shift towards more complex placements.
findings.matters: Large, sustained cost inflation in a demand-led provision type signals a market-wide issue (provider costs, market tightness) rather than a single-council procurement issue; pricing discipline becomes critical.
findings.figures: £21.047m forecast; 404 FTE vs 254 FTE (59% increase); average cost from £34.3k to £52.0k (51% increase)
findings.quote: Independent specialist placements are the largest single year-on-year driver, increasing by £2.979m to £21.047m. The pressure reflects both volume and price: the current forecast supports approximately 404 FTE placements, compared with 254 FTE in FY 2020-21, while the average placement cost has risen from approximately £34.3k to £52.0k.

findings.paper_title: Item 4. DSG Budget Monitoring FY 2026-27 - Oct 2026
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to reach £19.368m by 31 March 2027, after an in-year overspend of £16.112m
findings.detail: Brought-forward deficit of £3.255m (working assumption includes 90% write-off through High Needs Stability Grant) plus £16.112m in-year pressure. The paper states the write-off 'does not address the underlying in-year gap between High Needs funding and expenditure' and that 'the continuing rise in the annual High Needs pressure therefore remains the principal risk to the sustainability of the DSG.'
findings.matters: Growing cumulative deficits ultimately draw on general fund reserves; government write-offs do not address structural funding gaps, leaving councils with material medium-term balance sheet pressures.
findings.figures: £3.255m brought forward (after assumed 90% write-off); £16.112m in-year pressure; £19.368m projected closing balance
findings.quote: After the forecast in-year pressure of £16.112m, the cumulative DSG deficit would increase to £19.368m by 31 March 2027 at the current rate.

daily_post.headline: National pay award of 3.3% exceeds budgeted provision of 2.5%, creating £1.2m pressure on contingency
daily_post.lead: An inflation contingency already containing only limited headroom above expected inflation is now reduced by an unfunded pay award, constraining the council's ability to manage other in-year price pressures.
